topic: How bicycle brakes work, built one part at a time from a bike with no brakes

hook.say: 80 kilos. 32 kilometers per hour. Just an 8% hill. And your bike has no brakes. Congratulations!

beats.say: Holding that speed means shedding about 560 watts. Your shoes can't. So you press a rubber pad on the rim. That's a rim brake.
beats.label: RIM BRAKE
beats.creates: you can't reach the wheel while riding

beats.say: But you can't reach the wheel while riding. So a cable runs to a lever on your handlebar. Now squeezing stops you.
beats.label: LEVER + CABLE

beats.say: Then it rains, and wet rims brake badly. So you squeeze a disc on the hub, away from the rim. That's a disc brake.
beats.label: DISC BRAKE

beats.say: But cables stretch and drag. So you swap the cable for fluid in a sealed hose, like a syringe. That's hydraulic.
beats.label: HYDRAULIC LINE

beats.say: On a long descent, heat weakens the brakes. So you fit a bigger rotor, which sheds heat better.
beats.label: BIGGER ROTOR

payoff.say: You built a modern disc brake. It turns that hill into heat. Your shoes can retire.
payoff.title: YOU BUILT A DISC BRAKE.
payoff.subtitle: ONE PROBLEM AT A TIME

ask.say: Save this for your next big hill.

original_element: The build itself: each brake part is added on screen to fix the exact problem the previous part caused.

sources.claim: 80 kg rider+bike, 8% grade, 8.94 m/s (32.2 km/h) gives about 559 W of energy to dissipate (upper bound: ignores air drag and rolling resistance)
sources: Proceedings (MDPI) 2020, 'Bicycle Disc Brake Thermal Performance...' (559 W for 80 kg, 8%, 8.94 m/s)

sources.claim: Braking presses pads on a rim or rotor; friction turns motion into heat
sources.source: BikeRadar, 'Bike brakes explained'; Explain that Stuff, 'Brakes' (both read 2026-11-10)

sources.claim: Rim brakes are much weaker in the wet; disc rotor sits on the hub, away from the rim
sources.source: Cyclingnews, 'Disc brakes vs rim brakes'; Ribble Cycles blog 'Disc brake vs rim brake'; BikeRadar (read 2026-11-10)

sources.claim: Cable brakes lose force to cable stretch and housing friction; hydraulic fluid is essentially incompressible so nearly all lever force arrives
sources.source: Velo (Outside), 'Hydraulic vs mechanical disc brakes'; BikeTips 'Mechanical vs hydraulic disc brakes'; BikeRadar (read 2026-11-10)

sources.claim: Larger rotors shed heat better and lower the chance of brake fade on long descents
sources.source: BikeRadar 'Trail Tech: Disc brake rotor size'; Competitive Cyclist 'How to choose brake rotor size' (read 2026-11-10)
